content: Statistical analysis of the data was conducted using the OpenMeta[Analyst] software. To evaluate sensitivity and specificity, a bivariate analysis employing maximum likelihood estimation and 95% confidence intervals was utilized. Likelihood ratios were derived directly from the pooled sensitivity and specificity values. Forest plots were employed to visually assess heterogeneity among the studies. Stratified analyses were performed to compare studies that adhered to the manufacturer-recommended cut-off values with those that used lower cut-off thresholds. Additionally, comparisons were made between studies that stored dried blood spot (DBS) samples under cold chain conditions (refrigerated or frozen) and those that stored samples at ambient or higher temperatures. The risk of bias was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. Two independent reviewers conducted a GRADE assessment to evaluate the quality of the included studies. A total of 240 studies were initially identified, of which 108 met the inclusion criteria for the review. However, only nine studies provided sufficient data for inclusion in the meta-analysis. These studies collectively analyzed 370 positive samples out of 1,516 total samples. Storage conditions varied across studies, with three studies storing samples under refrigerated or frozen conditions, six studies storing samples at ambient or higher temperatures, and one study not specifying storage conditions. Some studies adjusted the test cut-off values for DBS samples, while others adhered to the manufacturer-recommended thresholds. Testing for HBsAg using DBS demonstrated good diagnostic accuracy when compared to reference tests using plasma or serum. Storage conditions, including temperature ranges from -20°C to 33°C and storage durations from overnight to 180 days, were evaluated. In general, storage at room temperature or higher (30–33°C) did not significantly affect test accuracy compared to cold chain storage. However, two studies noted a decline in sensitivity when samples were stored for more than 15 days at room temperature or for more than 63 days at room temperature, with reductions in both sensitivity and specificity. Stratified analyses comparing cold chain storage (2–8°C or frozen) with ambient or higher temperatures (30–33°C) were conducted for five studies. Other studies were excluded due to insufficient data to determine sensitivity or specificity at specific temperature conditions. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses suggested that the cut-off values for determining test positivity should be lower for DBS samples compared to plasma or serum samples. This adjustment is likely due to the smaller blood volume used in DBS (typically 50 µL per 12 mm diameter circle). Studies that used lower cut-off values for DBS demonstrated higher sensitivity without significant loss of specificity compared to those using manufacturer-recommended thresholds. Each test kit should be individually evaluated to determine its optimal cut-off value for DBS, which is typically lower than the serum test cut-off to enhance sensitivity. The risk of bias assessment revealed that several studies did not employ random or consecutive sampling methods or used study populations inconsistent with the target screening population. The lack of standardized cut-off values for HBsAg testing using DBS led some studies to adjust cut-offs based on ROC curve results, potentially introducing bias. These studies were deemed to have a high risk of bias in the index test domain. However, the included studies demonstrated a low risk of bias in the reference test and flow/timing domains. The GRADE analysis indicated that the evidence provided by the included studies was of moderate quality for assessing sensitivity and specificity. This systematic review and meta-analysis provide moderate-quality evidence supporting the acceptable accuracy of DBS for HBsAg testing compared to plasma samples. DBS may be a viable option for HBV screening in settings with limited access to venipuncture or inadequate infrastructure for plasma sample preparation and transport. While DBS appears stable and accurate under higher temperature and humidity conditions, prolonged storage at room temperature or above (>14 days) may negatively impact accuracy. Further operational research is needed to validate DBS use under real-world conditions, including high humidity environments. The use of DBS may require adjustments to cut-off values to maintain sensitivity, given the smaller blood volume used. Stratified analyses showed that DBS with lower cut-off values achieved higher sensitivity without significant loss of specificity. Each test kit should be validated for its ideal DBS cut-off value, which will typically differ from serum test cut-offs. Validation of DBS with commercially available HBsAg tests and determination of appropriate cut-off values are essential. Key limitations of this review include the small number of studies and variability in storage conditions and cut-off values. Future research should focus on operational studies using field specimens prepared and stored under real-world conditions. These studies should ideally use capillary whole blood to prepare DBS, employ commonly available filter paper types, and compare multiple commercial test kits and storage conditions. Expanded use of HBsAg testing is critical for improving HBV diagnosis and treatment globally. While commercial HBsAg rapid diagnostic tests are useful in certain contexts, the ability to use DBS for improved sample preparation, storage, and transport in decentralized testing settings may help expand the reach of this important diagnostic tool.
